title: Agent API
one_liner: A FastAPI chat agent on one provider-agnostic LLM door that can call the sales-forecast service as a tool, with no key in source.
body_html:
Agent API

Brief

The course exercise was a thin FastAPI wrapper that forwarded text to Gemini, with an API key hardcoded as a fallback. This version keeps the POST /ask contract and the CLI loop, but reads keys from the environment only, runs on Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini without code changes, works offline for tests and demos, and does one thing a proxy cannot: it decides when to call the restaurant sales forecast service and answers from the result.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv matches every other service in the repo
Model or core logic common/llm.py (complete, complete_json) + a two-step tool loop in agent.py one door for keys and providers; the loop is plain functions, easy to test
Interface FastAPI POST /ask, GET /health, HTML chat page on /, client.py CLI same shape as the original, plus a page an interviewer can click
Data capstone3-sales-forecast on :8104 (/forecast) and its models/metrics.json the tool has something real to call and a file to fall back on
Tests pytest + TestClient, 9 tests, all offline the backend is mocked, the metrics file is a temp file

Libraries used

fastapi (routes and validation), uvicorn (server), jinja2 (chat page), requests (tool call to :8104 and the CLI client), anthropic / openai / google-genai (provider SDKs, imported lazily by common/llm.py only when that provider is chosen), pytest + httpx (tests), ruff (lint).

How it was built

  1. Read agent.py, test_agent.py and Agent.ipynb from the course folder; noted the hardcoded key and the single Gemini call. The key was not copied anywhere.
  2. Replaced the Gemini client with common/llm.py: provider and model from env, offline deterministic fallback. Keys from env only, provider-agnostic.
  3. Added the tool loop: decide() asks for JSON (tool, store, days) through complete_json; forecast() calls POST :8104/forecast with a 15 s timeout and falls back to metrics.json; metrics() reads the scores; the model is asked again with the result. Offline, decide() is a keyword parser so the loop still runs.
  4. Kept the CLI loop as client.py (port 8105, one-shot mode added, shows which tool ran).
  5. Built the chat page on common/ui.css: provider badge (.on only with a key), message list, three one-click examples, ids #input, #run, #result.
  6. Wrote the tests with the backend mocked and LLM_PROVIDER=offline forced; just test runs ruff then pytest.

Results

No model is trained here; the tests are the result.

Test Proves
health {"ok": true, "service": "agent-api", "model_loaded": false} with no key
ask offline a response comes back with provider offline, no tool call for a plain question
tool loop, mocked backend the forecast tool is called exactly once with ("Bob's Diner", 5); the reply quotes the total (500)
backend down the tool falls back to metrics.json and the reply says so
metrics tool the winner and its RMSE are read from the file
chat page badge, examples and stable ids are present

Live (both services up, offline provider): "Forecast sales for Bob's Diner for the next 14 days" returns about 6,366 units from the XGBoost model on :8104 in under a second.

Demo

  • Run: just setup && just up (and the same in ../capstone3-sales-forecast), open http://localhost:8105/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: click the first example (forecast tool, live source shown under the reply); click the second (metrics tool); type anything else (plain answer); stop :8104 and repeat the first (fallback source).
  • Video clip: demo/clips/agent-api.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: the three example buttons on the page; just demo runs the same three through client.py.

Limits and next steps

  • One tool round per question and no conversation memory; a production agent would keep history and allow several rounds.
  • Offline replies are summaries, not prose; they exist so the loop is testable without a key.
  • The fallback forecast is a flat 28-day mean, labelled as such; it is a safety net, not a model.
  • Next: stream replies, add a history(store) tool against the EDA tables, and record provider latency in the response.

title: Vehicle detection and Tesla autopilot safety
one_liner: A Keras model that names the main vehicle in a traffic-camera frame and boxes it, plus the data analysis of Tesla's fatal-crash sheet.
body_html:
Vehicle detection and Tesla autopilot safety

Brief

Intelligent transport systems need to count, track and classify vehicles from roadside cameras in real time. Part 1 asks for a deep-learning model that says what kind of vehicle is in a frame (car, bus, pickup, truck, bicycle and so on) and where it is, as a rectangle. Part 2 asks what the public "Tesla Deaths" sheet says about Autopilot and road safety: events by year, country and model, who died, and how many Autopilot deaths are claimed versus verified. Solved means a page where you drop a camera frame and get a labelled box, and a page that answers the safety questions with numbers that can be checked.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv TensorFlow 2.21 runs natively on Apple silicon
Model or core logic Keras: MobileNetV2 (ImageNet) + class head + box head; GIoU + L1 box loss Pretrained features are what make a five-minute CPU run useful; the notebook's from-scratch CNN is kept as --backbone custom
Interface FastAPI + one HTML page per part (plain JS canvas draws the box) No build step, scriptable ids #input #run #result
Data 5,626 traffic-camera images with 17,967 boxes (MIO-TCD style, 142 MB zip); Tesla sheet 294 events From the Caltech dataset folder, read only; images extracted to ../data/
Tests pytest + FastAPI TestClient, 8 tests, offline Health, metrics, predict on a real image, bad upload, page ids, safety tables and totals

Libraries used

tensorflow (Keras model, training, saved .keras file), numpy (arrays, IoU), pandas (labels and the Tesla sheet), pillow (image decode and resize), fastapi + uvicorn (HTTP service), jinja2 (the two pages), python-multipart (file upload), matplotlib (three PNG charts on the safety page), pytest + httpx (tests), ruff (lint and format), opencv-python-headless (installed for parity with the notebook; the code path uses Pillow).

How it was built

  1. Read the notebook: first 2,000 CSV rows, 224 px resize, a five-block CNN with a softmax head and a 4-number box head, sparse_categorical_crossentropy + mse, 10 epochs, 64.5% val accuracy and a box MAE of 202 px because it regressed raw pixel coordinates without scaling anything.
  2. Inspected the data: the CSV lists 110,593 image ids but only 5,626 images exist; filtered to those. The notebook's row-per-box setup repeats an image with different targets, so each image now contributes one target, its largest box, normalised by its own width and height.
  3. Kept the notebook's two-head shape but put an ImageNet MobileNetV2 under it (authorised for the 10-minute budget), with the box head predicting centre and size through sigmoids so the box is always valid, and 1 - GIoU + L1 instead of MSE. Left-right flip augmentation and sqrt inverse-frequency class weights, because car is 59% of the targets.
  4. Training in two phases (frozen backbone, then blocks 10-16 unfrozen at a low learning rate) with early stopping; --quick uses 4,500 images, --full all 5,626.
  5. Two bugs found by looking at raw outputs, not just the loss: a sorted-corner GIoU let the model learn y1 and y2 swapped (IoU 0.0 with a plausible MAE), and an unnormalised head saturated its sigmoids in the frozen phase. Fixed by the centre/size parametrisation and BatchNorm in the head.
  6. Evaluation writes models/metrics.json with baselines next to every number (majority class, mean box) and a second IoU against the best-matching labelled box, to separate "wrong vehicle" from "loose box". src/evaluate.py recomputes it from the saved model.
  7. Part 2: stripped column names, dropped the 13 footer rows of totals, turned '-' into 0, re-derived Year from Date, folded Holland into Netherlands, then grouped by year, country, state, model and weekday. The recomputed totals match the sheet's own footer row exactly.
  8. FastAPI service with the shared dark UI, one-click samples, canvas box drawing, /health, /metrics, /safety; justfile; tests; this brief.

Results

Quick mode on an M4 Max (CPU), 4,500 images, 11 epochs, 307 s:

metric value what it means
val accuracy 73.0% majority-class baseline 58.7%; the notebook reported 64.5%
val macro F1 0.47 rare classes drag it down; bus 0.90, car 0.86, pickup 0.48 recall
mean box IoU 0.245 mean-box baseline 0.086; a real detector would be 0.6+
boxes with IoU >= 0.5 11% the box is on the right vehicle but loose
best-match IoU 0.249 almost the same, so misses are imprecision, not another vehicle
box MAE 33 px at 224 notebook: 202 px

Part 2: 294 fatal events, 353 deaths, 2013 to January 2023; 73% in the USA, California 91 events; 2022 the peak with 93 events; Autopilot claimed in 35 events (38 deaths), verified in 16 (19 deaths, 5.4% of all deaths), 27 deaths once NHTSA SGO reports are added; model known for only 38% of events.

Demo

  • Run: just setup && just train && just up, open http://localhost:8101/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) click Detect vehicle with the preselected sample: "bus 100%" and a box around the articulated bus; (2) click the other thumbnails or drop your own road photo; (3) open Part 2: Tesla safety analysis and look at the amber (claimed) versus teal (verified) chart and the headline tiles; (4) just demo prints the JSON for one sample.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/capstone1-vehicle-detection.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: six dataset frames served at /sample/{id} and shown as thumbnails; sample 00000001 gives bus 100%, 00000007 and 00000123 give car 98%, 00000042 (a near-empty road) gives car 34%, which is the model saying it is unsure.

Limits and next steps

  • One box per image, the largest vehicle; the data has up to a dozen vehicles per frame and a production model would predict all of them (anchor-based or DETR-style head, 512 px input).
  • IoU 0.25 is honest for five minutes of CPU training; just train-full adds the remaining images and up to 30 fine-tune epochs, which should give a few points, not a new regime.
  • Classes with fewer than a dozen validation images (motorcycle, single-unit truck, non-motorized vehicle, pedestrian) have near-zero recall; they need oversampling or more data.
  • The MobileNetV2 weights download once from Keras on the first just train; after that the whole project is offline. Tests never touch the network.
  • The Tesla sheet counts events with no miles-driven denominator, so it supports "how many" and "where", not "is Autopilot safer".

title: Historical structures classifier
one_liner: Upload a photo of a church or monument detail and a transfer-learned CNN names which of ten architectural elements it is, with a confidence.
body_html:
Historical structures classifier

Brief

A government tourism agency wants to monitor centuries-old buildings and flag the ones that need maintenance. Step one is knowing what a photo shows: an altar, an apse, a bell tower, a column, the inside or outside of a dome, a flying buttress, a gargoyle, stained glass or a vault. The task (Caltech CTME capstone 2, part 1) is a TensorFlow model that predicts that category from an image, built with transfer learning because ten thousand photos is not enough to train a CNN from scratch. "Solved" is a model that gets most held-out test photos right and a way for a non-engineer to try it.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv pinned, reproducible, TensorFlow wheels available for Apple silicon
Model or core logic TensorFlow 2.21 / Keras 3, MobileNetV2 ImageNet backbone (frozen) + Dense(256)/Dropout(0.5)/softmax head the notebook's head on a backbone that trains on a laptop CPU in seconds instead of VGG16's hours
Interface FastAPI + one HTML page (Jinja2, no build step) upload or click a sample, top-3 with bars, live metrics; shares common/ui.css
Data 10,235 training JPEGs in 10 class folders, 1,473 test images in a separate folder (154 MB, read in place) the course dataset; corrupt files detected and excluded
Tests pytest + FastAPI TestClient, 9 tests, offline, 3 s health contract, metrics, predictions for three classes, bad input, gallery page

Libraries used

tensorflow/keras (backbone, head, training, saving .keras), pillow (decode, corrupt-image check, resize), numpy (image arrays, per-class accuracy, confusion matrix), matplotlib (accuracy and loss curves), fastapi + uvicorn + python-multipart + jinja2 (the service and page), pytest + httpx (tests), ruff (lint), pandas (installed for parity with the other capstones; not needed by this one).

How it was built

  1. Read the two course notebooks and the problem statement. The notebook plots 8 images per class with OpenCV, removes truncated images with PIL (Image.open + load, os.remove on failure), loads VGG16 without its top, freezes it, adds Flatten -> Dense(256, relu) -> Dropout(0.5) -> Dense(10, softmax), compiles with Adam and categorical cross-entropy, stops early on val_accuracy, trains at 224px without augmentation and then with it (rotation 20°, shifts 0.2, shear 0.2, zoom 0.2, flip), and plots the curves. It used the test folder as the validation set.
  2. Data scan (src/structures/data.py): same readability check, but the source folders are never written to; unreadable files are listed and skipped (3 in the test set, 0 in training) and counts per class are logged and saved to models/dataset_scan.json. Images are resized once into a cached array under data/capstone2/.
  3. Split: 15% of the training folder held out per class for validation; the test folder is used only once, at the end. This is the main change from the notebook, which validated on the test set.
  4. Model (src/structures/model.py): the notebook's head, optimiser, loss and callbacks kept; backbone switched to MobileNetV2 (EfficientNetB0 selectable) with the input scaling inside the model. Added the problem statement's "stop at a chosen validation accuracy" callback next to EarlyStopping. Augmentation is the notebook's ImageDataGenerator settings as Keras layers, wrapped around the model only while training.
  5. Training (src/train.py): --quick (150 images per class, 160px, 2 plain + 2 augmented epochs) and --full (everything, 224px, up to 10 + 10 with early stopping). Both phases are run as in the notebook; the weights with the best validation accuracy across phases are saved. Outputs: model, classes, metrics (train/val/test, per class, confusion matrix, epoch history, wall time), curves, and one test image per class for the gallery.
  6. Service (app.py): /, /predict (file upload or sample=<class>), /health, /metrics, /curves.png.
  7. Tests and justfile: setup, train, train-full, run, up, down, test, demo.

Results

Quick mode on this machine (M4 Max, CPU), models/metrics-quick.json:

Number Value Meaning
Test accuracy 89.3% 1,473 never-seen images from the separate test folder; chance is 10%
Best validation accuracy 93.6% 220 held-out training images, baseline phase, epoch 2 (the saved weights)
Train accuracy at that epoch 89.6% below validation because dropout is on while training
Per class (test) flying_buttress 98.7, altar 97.1, dome(outer) 96.4, gargoyle 92.0, stained_glass 92.0, dome(inner) 90.7, bell_tower 90.0, vault 89.0, column 79.0, apse 52.6 apse (57 test images) is confused with bell_tower and column
Cost 1,280 training images, 4 epochs, 13 s training, 18 s wall time 150 images per class is enough for a frozen backbone to reach ~90%

The notebook reached 0.90 validation accuracy with VGG16 on all images (validating on the test folder). A good number for this dataset with a fine-tuned backbone is mid-90s; the quick model is within a few points of the notebook on 15% of the data.

Full mode (just train-full, the model now deployed), models/metrics-full.json:

Number Value Meaning
Test accuracy 93.3% same 1,473 test images; the notebook reported 0.90 with VGG16
Best validation accuracy 95.6% 1,535 held-out training images, baseline phase, epoch 4 (the saved weights)
Per class (test) dome(outer) 98.8, gargoyle 97.1, stained_glass 96.9, altar 95.7, bell_tower 95.3, column 95.2, vault 92.1, dome(inner) 90.7, flying_buttress 78.2, apse 61.4 apse is still the weak class; flying buttresses are often photographed with the whole facade
Cost 8,700 training images, 14 epochs (early stopping in both phases), 12.2 min on CPU augmentation peaked at 93.6% validation, below the plain phase, so the plain weights were kept

Demo

  • Run: just setup && just up, open http://localhost:8102/ (just train rebuilds a quick model in ~25 s; just train-full the full one in ~12 min).
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) click gargoyle in the sample gallery; the result card shows the image, the predicted class, its confidence and the top-3 bars, with a pill confirming the test label. (2) Click apse, then scroll to the per-class table: apse is the weak class (61.4% full, 52.6% quick), the gallery images are the model's most confident correct test images, so the table is the honest number. (3) Drop any photo of a cathedral window, a dome or a gargoyle from your own files onto the page; it classifies on drop. (4) Look at the curves: the dashed line is where augmentation switches on; validation accuracy drops after it in both modes, so the script kept the plain-phase weights.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/capstone2-structures.webm (recorded by just demo-video at the root; coordinator owns it).
  • Sample inputs: static/samples/<class>.jpg, one per class, taken from the test set. Expected result: the matching class at >99% for all ten (they were selected as confident correct predictions).
  • Script hooks: #input (file input), #run (Classify button), #result (result container); gallery buttons carry data-sample="<class>" and classify on click without an upload.

Limits and next steps

  • just train (quick, 25 s) rebuilds a 15%-of-data demo model at 160px and overwrites the deployed full model; just train-full (12 min) restores the 93.3% one. Both metrics files are kept side by side.
  • Augmentation hurts in a short run on a frozen backbone with a Flatten head; the script keeps the better phase. A production version would fine-tune the top blocks at a low learning rate and use global average pooling.
  • Apse and column are weak; they need more data or a backbone fine-tune, and a confusion-matrix view in the UI.
  • Validation here is split from training data, so the numbers are not directly comparable to the notebook's 0.90, which validated on the test set.
  • CPU inference (~50 ms per image) and a single process: fine for a demo, not for a queue of maintenance photos.

title: Tourism recommender (Capstone 2, Part 2)
one_liner: Explores 437 Indonesian tourist spots and 10k user ratings, then recommends places to a known user or to someone who only states a category, city and budget, with a reason for every pick.
body_html:
Tourism recommender (Capstone 2, Part 2)

Brief

A government tourism agency wants to market Indonesia's five big cities better. It has a catalogue of 437 attractions, 300 tourists' demographics and 10,000 star ratings, and asks two things: what do the data say about who visits what, and can a recommender point each tourist to places they have not seen yet. "Solved" is an analysis with clear answers (which city for nature, which spots and categories are loved) and a working engine that returns ten unvisited places per user with an explanation.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv one lockfile, same across the suite
Model or core logic pandas + scikit-learn: cosine kNN, TruncatedSVD, TF-IDF content model, rank fusion small data (300 x 437), fits in two seconds, fully inspectable
Interface FastAPI + Jinja2 HTML, shared common/ui.css no build step, scriptable ids for the demo video
Data tourism_with_id.xlsx (437 places), user.csv (300), tourism_rating.csv (10,000 rows -> 9,597 pairs) the course dataset, read-only from DATA_ROOT
Tests pytest + FastAPI TestClient, 9 tests, offline health, metrics, recommend contracts, page states

Libraries used

pandas (cleaning, group-bys, the user x place pivot), numpy (similarity matrices and predictions), scikit-learn (cosine_similarity, TruncatedSVD, TfidfVectorizer), scipy (sparse stacking of the content features), openpyxl (read the xlsx), matplotlib (7 PNG charts), fastapi + uvicorn (API and pages), jinja2 (templates), pydantic (request validation), httpx (demo script and TestClient), pytest, ruff.

How it was built

  1. Read the solution notebook (62 cells) and the problem statement. Kept its cleaning exactly: drop the two Unnamed columns, Coordinate and Time_Minutes; strip and capitalise Category. Added one step it missed: 403 duplicate (user, place) rating pairs are averaged, which its pivot did implicitly.
  2. Rebuilt the notebook's EDA as code that writes models/eda.json and seven charts: age bands, home cities, category counts, category per city, weighted ratings, loved cities and categories, and a new rating-signal chart. The "weighted average rating" is an IMDb-style Bayesian average (m = median votes per place), shown next to the notebook's plain mean; both put Keraton Surabaya first.
  3. Recommender. The notebook's user-based Pearson/cosine neighbour scoring became a proper rating predictor (user kNN), joined by item kNN and TruncatedSVD on the mean-centred matrix. A content model was added because the problem statement asks for recommendations from a current place or interests: one-hot category and city, log price, TF-IDF of the description.
  4. Evaluation: 20% random hold-out of the rating pairs; RMSE for every predictor and three baselines; hit-rate@10, precision@5 and recall@10 for each route against held-out ratings >= 4, with the random expectation printed beside them.
  5. Found that no predictor beats the global mean on four seeds and a full sweep of k, SVD rank and shrinkage. Checked why: the ratings are uniform over 1–5, and shuffling them changes nothing about the spread of per-place means. Stopped tuning; added shrinkage to kNN so it is not worse than the baseline, and reported the result as is.
  6. Interface: a user picker (user 1 preselected so the first load shows results), route switch, interests form with sample buttons, reason and source pill per place, metric tiles from metrics.json, and a findings page with the charts and the plain-words answers.
  7. Tests and lint, then just up / just demo / just down as the proof path.

Results

From models/metrics.json, quick mode (identical to full; 2 s on this machine), seed 42:

Metric Value Baseline Meaning
RMSE, SVD rank 2 1.384 1.363 global mean lower is better; a real dataset would show the model 10–20% under the baseline
RMSE, user kNN / item kNN 1.384 / 1.382 1.383 user mean neighbour votes add nothing here
hit-rate@10, hybrid 5.4% 6.5% random share of 280 test users with a liked held-out place in their top 10
precision@5, collaborative 0.71% 0.67% random liked held-out places among the first five

The honest reading: the rating file is synthetic noise (entropy 2.315 of 2.322 bits, per-place mean spread 0.308 vs 0.299 after shuffling), so collaborative filtering has nothing to learn and the numbers sit on the baseline. The content route is the one that produces sensible, explainable picks because it uses the real catalogue. The EDA conclusions (Bandung for nature, Keraton Surabaya top, amusement parks then nature preserves most loved) match the solution notebook exactly.

Demo

  • Run: just setup && just train && just up, open http://localhost:8103/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) the page opens on user 1 with ten picks already shown; open "Places they already rated" to see what is excluded; (2) set Route to "Content only", press Recommend, read the reasons ("Similar to Museum Bahari Jakarta which you rated 5/5; same category and city"); (3) press "Nature, Bandung, ≤20k" for an interests query; (4) open "Findings and charts" and scroll to the rating-signal chart.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/capstone2-tourism-recommender.webm (recorded by just demo-video at the root).
  • Sample inputs: user ids 1, 42, 286 (buttons on the page); interests "Cagar alam + Bandung + 20000" returns Bukit Jamur, Sanghyang Heuleut, Rainbow Garden, Curug Batu Templek, Tafso Barn. just demo prints the same calls from the shell.

Limits and next steps

  • Ratings are synthetic, so the collaborative metrics say nothing about tourist taste; the harness is ready for real ratings.
  • The problem statement mentions "current tourist location"; the content route handles a place name via ContentModel.similar_places, but the page does not expose it yet, and the latitude/longitude columns are unused. A "near me" route by haversine distance is the next step.
  • TF-IDF without stemming on Indonesian text; category and city weights were set by hand, not learned.
  • Single process, model in memory, no auth or caching; a production version would precompute per-user lists nightly and serve them from a store.

title: Restaurant sales forecast
one_liner: Three years of restaurant item sales explored and forecast per store and item with XGBoost, random forest, linear regression and an LSTM, served on a dashboard.
body_html:
Restaurant sales forecast

Brief

Fresh Analytics wants to understand and predict demand for items across six restaurants so that purchasing, staffing and planning can run on numbers instead of guesses. The data is 1,096 days of sales for 100 items. Solved means: the patterns (day of week, month, quarter, store, item, price versus volume) are stated with numbers, three regression models plus a deep model are compared on the last six months, and the best one gives a forecast for any store and item over any horizon up to a year.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv TensorFlow and XGBoost wheels, same as the rest of the repo
Model or core logic scikit-learn LR and RF, XGBoost, Keras LSTM; pandas feature engineering the notebook's four models; XGBoost won on the holdout
Interface FastAPI + one Jinja2 HTML page, inline SVG chart, no build step loads in a second, scriptable ids, works offline
Data sales.csv 109,600 rows, items.csv 100, resturants.csv 6, read from DATA_ROOT the capstone dataset, read-only
Tests pytest + TestClient, 7 tests, offline health, metrics, forecast shape and bounds, dashboard

Libraries used

pandas / numpy (merge, features, aggregation), scikit-learn (LinearRegression, RandomForestRegressor, metrics, scaler, one-hot), xgboost (XGBRegressor with early stopping), tensorflow (Keras LSTM), matplotlib (eight EDA charts on the dark surface), joblib (model file), fastapi + uvicorn + jinja2 (API and page), pytest + httpx (tests), ruff (lint).

How it was built

  1. Extracted the 164 notebook cells and the problem statement PDF; listed every table and chart the notebook produces and the three model scores it reports (LR 244.21, RF 59.91, XGB 72.30 RMSE; LSTM MAPE 1.34).
  2. src/data.py merges the three CSVs exactly as the notebook does (sales → items → restaurants) and adds revenue.
  3. src/eda.py recomputes every notebook table into findings.json with sentences generated from the numbers, and draws eight charts with the shared dark palette.
  4. Changed the model framing: the notebook forecasts one daily total, which cannot answer "how many for store 4 next week". The models here train on the date x item panel with store, item, price and kcal as features, and are scored both per row and on the daily total so the notebook's numbers remain comparable. A replica of the notebook's own framing is trained too and matches it to the decimal for LR.
  5. Kept the notebook's holdout (last six months) and metrics (RMSE, MAE, R², plus MAPE). XGBoost early-stops on the last 90 days of the training window, not on the holdout.
  6. LSTM as in the notebook (12-day window, 100 units, MinMax on revenue, recursive 184-day evaluation), with two changes: a tanh cell instead of relu, which diverged when fed its own output, and a fixed seed with deterministic ops.
  7. app.py serves the forecast (POST /forecast), metrics, health and the dashboard; the page runs a forecast on load.
  8. Tests, justfile (setup, train, train-full, run, up, down, test, demo), README.

Results

Quick mode (just train, 49 s), holdout 2021-07-01 to 2021-12-31, scores on the daily total over all items:

Model RMSE (units/day) MAE MAPE R²
Linear regression 136.4 98.3 25.1% 0.71
Random forest 86.1 69.5 15.4% 0.89
XGBoost (winner) 59.9 47.5 9.9% 0.94
LSTM recursive, $ revenue 6,088 5,086 116.8% -5.3
LSTM one step ahead, $ revenue 979 779 15.6% 0.83

Full mode (just train-full, 3 min 40 s): random forest 84.9 / 68.4 / 15.2%, XGBoost 59.9 / 47.6 / 9.6% (still the winner), LSTM recursive 2,166 / 1,825 / 29.1% and one step ahead 825 / 646 / 12.7%. The notebook reported LR 244.21, RF 59.91, XGB 72.30 on its aggregate series and LSTM MAPE 1.34; the replica here gives 244.21, 60.34, 73.44 and 0.29 (full) / 1.17 (quick).

Daily totals run 175 to 1,201 units, so RMSE 60 is roughly a 10 percent error on a typical day; the notebook's best was 59.91 on the aggregate series. A good production number for daily restaurant demand is a MAPE under 10 percent, which XGBoost reaches here.

Demo

  • Run: just setup && just train && just up, open http://localhost:8104/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: the forecast for Bob's Diner over 30 days is already on screen; change the store to Fou Cher and the horizon to 90 (small numbers, as the EDA says); switch the model to LSTM for revenue; scroll to the score tiles and the eight captioned charts.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/capstone3-sales-forecast.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: the store and item dropdowns; just demo posts a 7-day forecast for Bob's Diner and a 5-day LSTM revenue forecast.

Limits and next steps

  • Tree models carry the 2021 level forward with the weekly and seasonal shape but no growth trend; a trend feature or a hybrid (trend model plus tree residuals) is the next step.
  • Bob's Diner is 99 percent of the volume; the other five stores are one or two units a day and their relative errors are large.
  • The recursive LSTM is unstable over 184 steps in the notebook and here; a direct multi-horizon model or a seq2seq would fix that.
  • Quick mode uses 40 trees / 300 rounds / 15 epochs; just train-full uses the notebook's settings and takes a few minutes.
  • No holidays, weather or promotions in the data; price never changes, so elasticity cannot be learned.

title: Dashboard
one_liner: One page that lists every capstone and portfolio service with a live status dot, the stack, an Open link and its brief.
body_html:
Dashboard

Brief

Fourteen services on fourteen ports are hard to show in an interview. The dashboard is the one address to open: it groups the five capstone services and the eight portfolio apps by target role, shows which are up right now, and opens each one or its brief in a click. "Solved" is an interviewer finding a working demo within ten seconds of opening http://localhost:5173/.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Node 24, React 18, Vite 5 same shape as the original portfolio dashboard, builds in seconds
Model or core logic none; src/services.js is the port map and card text one data file, tested against PLAN.md
Interface React single page on common/ui.css tokens same instrument panel as every other service
Data PLAN.md port table, public/briefs.json from just briefs no duplicated facts
Tests vitest (tests/portmap.test.js) plus npm run build fails when the page and the plan disagree

Libraries used

react and react-dom (the page), vite (dev server and build, pinned to 5173 with strictPort), vitest (the port-map test), @vitejs/plugin-react (JSX).

How it was built

  1. Read the PLAN.md port table and wrote PORT_MAP verbatim; wrote the test first so drift fails the build.
  2. Wrote the thirteen one-liners from each project's original README and the three capstone problem statements.
  3. Built the probe: CORS fetch of /health then /, falling back to mode: 'no-cors' so an opaque answer counts as up, a 5xx shows amber, a refused connection shows red; polled every ten seconds with a four-second timeout.
  4. Styled on common/ui.css (imported directly, not copied) with Space Grotesk, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono.
  5. Added the Brief panel: /briefs.json is optional; when present each card gets a Brief button that opens a dialog with that project's body and an Open link.
  6. Added justfile recipes and the root integration: tests/check_ports.py (status, response time, DOWN vs 5xx), tests/test_integration.py (INTEGRATION=1), tests/record_demo.py and tools/stitch.sh for the walkthrough video.

Results

Check Result
npm run build passes
vitest port map vs PLAN.md 6 tests pass
curl localhost:5173/ 200

The numbers that matter are on the other cards; this page has none of its own.

Demo

  • Run: just setup && just up, open http://localhost:5173/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: watch the "services up" count fill in; click Open on a green card; click Brief on any card; stop one service and watch its dot turn red within ten seconds.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/dashboard.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: none needed; the page polls on load.

Limits and next steps

  • The page cannot start or stop services; the hint box shows the just commands instead.
  • Status is reachability, not correctness: a port that answers anything counts as up.
  • Briefs render the collector's HTML; without just briefs the buttons are hidden.
  • A production version would serve the built dist/ behind the same reverse proxy as the services and drop the per-port links.

title: Telecom Churn Predictor
one_liner: Scores a telecom customer's churn risk with a Logistic Regression and a Random Forest trained once on synthetic data, in a Streamlit dashboard.
body_html:
Telecom Churn Predictor

Brief

Telecom operators lose revenue when customers switch providers, and the retention team cannot call everyone. This app predicts which customers are likely to churn so outreach goes to the riskiest first. "Solved" means a scored list with a model whose numbers are visible and reproducible, and a form to score one customer on demand.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv One venv per app, uv sync reproducible
Model or core logic scikit-learn: ColumnTransformer + LogisticRegression / RandomForestClassifier Interpretable baseline vs non-linear champion, both cheap to train
Interface Streamlit (shared dark theme from common/streamlit_theme.py) Dashboard with a form in a few lines; AppTest makes it testable
Data data/telecom_churn.csv, 1,000 synthetic rows from data_gen.py (seed 42) Same generator as the original portfolio
Tests pytest + streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest (6 tests) Training contract, scoring, unknown categories, UI renders and predicts

Libraries used

scikit-learn (pipelines, both models, metrics), pandas (data frames), joblib (model bundle), streamlit (UI and AppTest), numpy (data generation), ruff (lint), pytest.

How it was built

  1. Read the original app.py: it trained both models on every page load inside Streamlit, label-encoded categoricals with a single LabelEncoder reused across columns (so the encodings were wrong), and the prediction form sent a hand-built array with zeros for every categorical. The data generator and CSV were kept as they were.
  2. Moved training into train.py: proper ColumnTransformer with fixed category lists (features.py), stratified 80/20 split, accuracy / F1 / ROC-AUC for both models, Random Forest importances and LR coefficients, training means and standard deviations saved for the monitoring API's drift check. Champion chosen by ROC-AUC.
  3. Rebuilt the dashboard to load models/churn.joblib and models/metrics.json: comparison table, two charts, a form with every feature, "Use sample customer" and "Use safe customer" buttons, stable widget keys (input, run).
  4. Tests: training writes a bundle with sane metrics; the bundle scores a customer; an unknown category does not crash; AppTest renders the page, fills the form and gets a risk card.

Results

models/metrics.json, this machine, full data (training takes 3 s so there is no quick mode):

Model Accuracy F1 ROC-AUC
Logistic Regression (champion) 0.740 0.581 0.806
Random Forest 0.730 0.542 0.787

ROC-AUC 0.81 means the model ranks a random churner above a random non-churner 81% of the time. The original brief wanted accuracy > 0.80 and F1 > 0.70; the synthetic churn rule is noisy by construction (probability drawn from four indicators), so that target is not reachable on this data and the README says so instead of quoting it.

Demo

  • Run: just churn_predictor-setup && just churn_predictor-up, open http://127.0.0.1:8111/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) read the comparison table and say why LR is champion here; (2) look at the importance chart (tenure, charges, contract); (3) press "Use sample customer", then "Predict" for a red high-risk card; (4) press "Use safe customer", "Predict", green card; flip the contract to Month-to-month and watch it move.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__churn_predictor.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: the two buttons. Sample customer (3 months, $104, fiber, monthly) scores about 90% churn; safe customer (60 months, $30, DSL, two-year) scores under 10%.

Limits and next steps

  • The data is synthetic; nothing here says how the model would do on a real telecom book.
  • No calibration or threshold tuning: 0.5 is used as the cut, a retention team would pick a cut by call capacity.
  • Feature set is the generator's 11 columns; real data would add usage, support tickets and payment history.
  • Next: XGBoost with the same pipeline, SHAP for per-customer reasons, and this model is already served by model_monitoring_api (port 8115), which is the "deploy as an API with monitoring" step from the original plan.

title: Content Ops Assistant
one_liner: One campaign brief and four brand sliders become an email, a LinkedIn post and three ad variants, with the system prompt the sliders produce shown on the page.
body_html:
Content Ops Assistant

Brief

A marketing team rewrites the same launch brief for email, LinkedIn and ads, for different personas, and the tone drifts between writers. This assistant takes one brief, applies brand settings (tone, formality, length, persona, banned words) and writes every channel from the same prompt. Solved means a full channel set in seconds with a guardrail the team can read and adjust rather than a prompt hidden in code.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv same as the rest of the portfolio
Model or core logic BrandSettings -> build_system_prompt; common/llm.py complete per channel prompt is data, provider by env, deterministic offline copy
Interface Streamlit with common/streamlit_theme.py sliders in the sidebar, prompt and copy side by side; key="input", key="run"
Data SAMPLE_BRIEF (a feature launch with concrete numbers) one click to a result
Tests pytest (5) incl. AppTest smoke prompt logic, clamping, offline determinism, UI happy path

Libraries used

streamlit (UI, tabs, download button), anthropic / openai / google-genai (providers behind the shared door), pytest, ruff. No other runtime dependency.

How it was built

  1. Read the original app.py: a one-line f-string prompt per channel sent to OpenAI, a text banner instead of copy when no key, and an "Export to CSV" button that only showed a success message.
  2. Split the logic into content.py: BrandSettings (tone, formality 0-10, length, persona, banned words), build_system_prompt, per-channel format rules, and generate.
  3. Replaced the OpenAI call with common.llm.complete; added deterministic offline placeholder copy built from the brief and sliders, labelled [OFFLINE PLACEHOLDER <hash>].
  4. Built the page: sidebar sliders, the live system prompt under the brief, Use sample, Generate, one tab per channel, a real Markdown download, and a provider badge.
  5. Tests (prompt reflects sliders, clamping, determinism, validation, AppTest sample -> Generate), ruff, just recipes with a pid file.

Results

No numeric score; the brand guardrail is the visible prompt. The tests prove that every slider changes the prompt (Bold + formality 9 + Short vs Witty + 1 + Long give different prompts with the matching register and word budget), that offline output is identical across runs and changes when a slider changes, and that the UI reaches three filled output tabs from one click. With a key, a full set (three sequential Haiku calls) takes a few seconds, in line with the original under-15-seconds claim.

Demo

  • Run: just content_ops_assistant-setup && just content_ops_assistant-up, open http://localhost:8116/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) badge; (2) Use sample, read the prompt box; (3) set Tone to Bold and Formality to 2, watch the prompt change; (4) Generate, open the three tabs, download the Markdown.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__content_ops_assistant.webm.
  • Sample inputs: SAMPLE_BRIEF in content.py (the "Ledger Sync" launch). Offline, each tab starts with an [OFFLINE PLACEHOLDER ...] line and a subject line built from the first sentence of the brief.

Limits and next steps

  • Offline copy is a template, not writing; it exists so the demo runs with no key.
  • No automated tone or brand score; an LLM-as-judge check against the shown prompt is the next step.
  • The three channel calls run one after another; parallelising them is a small change.
  • Human review stays in the loop for anything that ships; the download is Markdown, not a CMS push.

title: Blueprint Analysis System
one_liner: Classifies an architectural drawing, reads its dimensions and room labels with EasyOCR, and segments rooms and walls with OpenCV, in a Gradio demo.
body_html:
Blueprint Analysis System

Brief

Construction and property teams get drawings as images and sort them by hand: which are floor plans, what are the dimensions, how many rooms. This pipeline takes one image and returns the drawing type, the text with its role (dimension, room label, scale), the enclosed regions and wall segments, and an annotated picture. "Solved" means an engineer can drop a drawing and get a reviewable JSON report in a few seconds.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv torch and easyocr pin cleanly on 3.11
Model or core logic EfficientNet-B0 (torchvision, ImageNet, frozen) + linear head trained on synthetic drawings; EasyOCR; OpenCV morphology + Hough Transfer learning gives a real classifier in a minute of CPU; OCR and segmentation need no training
Interface Gradio 5 Blocks mounted on FastAPI (shared theme in common/gradio_theme.py) Image in, images and JSON out, with /health
Data blueprint/samples.py draws 4 drawing types; 240 for training, 3 demo samples in samples/ No real blueprint dataset is bundled
Tests pytest (9 tests) samples, segmentation, both classifiers, text tagging, OCR (skips with reason if unavailable), detection skip note, full pipeline, app builds

Libraries used

torch + torchvision (EfficientNet-B0 features, linear head), easyocr (text detection and recognition), opencv-python-headless (drawing the samples, thresholds, morphology, contours, Hough lines), numpy, pillow (image handoff to Gradio), gradio (UI), fastapi + uvicorn (health endpoint and server), roboflow (optional extra, hosted detection), ruff, pytest.

How it was built

  1. Read the original five modules. Classifier, OCR and segmentation were sound designs but nothing ran: the package used relative imports from loose files, the classifier had ImageNet weights and an untrained 4-class head (blueprint_classifier.pth never existed), and detection returned random mock boxes without a key.
  2. Kept the segmentation algorithm as it was (adaptive threshold, horizontal/vertical opening, contours, HoughLinesP), added a fill-ratio filter so ragged regions are not rooms, and JSON output. Kept the OCR tagging regexes and added inversion for white-on-blue drawings.
  3. Wrote blueprint/samples.py to draw floor plans (recursive room splits, door gaps with swing arcs, labels, dimension lines, title block), elevations (storeys, windows, roofs, siding), sections (slabs, hatched cut walls, stairs) and site plans (dashed boundary, hatched footprint, trees, north arrow, setbacks), with augmentation.
  4. train.py: 60 drawings per class -> frozen EfficientNet-B0 features -> linear head, 60 epochs, held-out accuracy, confusion matrix, and the heuristic scored on the same split. load_classifier picks the head when models/classifier.pt exists and the heuristic otherwise, and every prediction carries its method.
  5. HeuristicClassifier: four hand-set rules on line statistics (round blobs = trees, thick dark bands = cut slabs, vertical/horizontal line ratio) so the pipeline runs with no model at all.
  6. Detection now only runs with ROBOFLOW_API_KEY; otherwise the report says it was skipped.
  7. Gradio app with one-click samples, two overlays, OCR table, JSON, and a "what is real" panel.

Results

models/classifier_metrics.json, this machine, 48 s of CPU training, 192 train / 48 test synthetic drawings:

Classifier Held-out accuracy
EfficientNet-B0 + head 1.00 (all four classes)
Heuristic rules 0.875

A good number on real scanned drawings would be above 0.9 across the four types; this 1.00 is on drawings from the same generator and only shows the head separates the synthetic styles. On the floor plan sample, OCR returns 14 regions including five dimensions in three notations and five room labels; segmentation returns 5 enclosed regions.

Demo

  • Run: just headstorm_blueprint-setup && just headstorm_blueprint-up, open http://127.0.0.1:8117/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) click the floor plan sample; (2) read the summary and the two overlays; (3) scroll to the OCR table and the JSON; (4) click the site plan sample and compare; (5) open "What is real and what is not".
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__headstorm_blueprint.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: samples/floor_plan.png (5 rooms, 5 dimensions, title block), samples/elevation.png, samples/site_plan.png (trees, north arrow, two setbacks in metres).

Limits and next steps

  • Every image is synthetic. The next real step is a few hundred labelled scanned drawings and fine-tuning the backbone.
  • Segmentation counts enclosed regions, not rooms: door gaps merge adjacent rooms, and elevations produce "rooms" from window panes. A wall-closing step or a learned segmentation model would fix both.
  • OCR reads SCALE 1:100 as SCALE 1.100; a blueprint-specific post-processor is easy and not done.
  • Roboflow detection is untested here (no key); the integration code follows the SDK but was not exercised.
  • First classification call on CPU is about 1 s and OCR 1-2 s per drawing; batch and GPU would change that.

title: MenuSync AI
one_liner: Turns a restaurant menu image into category, item and price rows with EasyOCR plus spatial line grouping, with a batch engine that writes JSON and CSV and scores itself against ground truth.
body_html:
MenuSync AI

Brief

A hospitality-tech client wants competitor pricing across more than a thousand restaurants, and the menus arrive as images. Typing them in does not scale. This pipeline reads a menu image and returns structured rows (restaurant, category, item, price) plus an annotated picture, and a batch engine does the same over a folder with an error log for the unreadable ones. "Solved" means a CSV a pricing analyst can load, with a measured accuracy next to it.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv easyocr/torch pin cleanly
Model or core logic EasyOCR (CRAFT detector + CRNN recogniser, English) and pure-Python spatial parsing OCR is the only learned part; the layout rules are testable without it
Interface Gradio 5 Blocks on FastAPI (shared theme in common/gradio_theme.py) Image in, table + annotated image + JSON out, batch button, /health
Data menusync/samples.py draws 5 menus (one two-column) with samples/ground_truth.json Makes extraction accuracy measurable
Tests pytest (11 tests) 6 on the parser with hand-made OCR tuples, 5 with real OCR on the samples (skip with reason if the model cannot load)

Libraries used

easyocr (text boxes with confidence), opencv-python-headless (image loading, grayscale, bilateral filter), pillow (drawing the synthetic menus, annotation overlay), numpy, pandas (the table in the UI), gradio (UI), fastapi + uvicorn (health and server), ruff, pytest.

How it was built

  1. Read the original three scripts: menu_parser.py had the line-grouping idea (sort by y, join within 15 px, split categories on all-caps, price if it has $ or a dot) but a fixed pixel threshold and no column handling; generate_samples.py drew one menu; batch_engine.py was a sleep loop printing a fake 98% success rate.
  2. Rewrote the parser as pure functions on OCR tuples (group_lines, structure, parse_price, split_columns) so the rules are unit-tested without EasyOCR: the line tolerance scales with the median text height, the price regex accepts EasyOCR's S for $, and the first non-category line is the restaurant.
  3. Drew five varied menus (fonts, paper colours, tilt, one two-column) and saved the ground truth with them, then wrote the evaluation (fuzzy item match, exact price match, category recall).
  4. First measured run: 87% item recall, 92% price accuracy; the two-column menu merged rows across columns. Added the column splitter (a centre-first scan for a box-free vertical band with prices on both sides).
  5. Second run: 100% items, 84.5% prices; the misses were $ read as 8 in one serif font. Added the page-level currency-glyph rule. Third run: 100% on all four measures.
  6. Batch engine with per-file try/except into errors.log, JSON + CSV + summary + eval outputs; Gradio UI with one-click samples, annotated overlay, table, JSON and a batch button.

Results

output/eval.json on this machine, five synthetic menus, 71 ground-truth items:

Measure Value
Item recall 1.00
Price accuracy on found items 1.00
Category recall 1.00
Files failed 0 of 5
Seconds per menu (CPU) 8.1 average (first file includes model load), 4-6 steady

The original write-up claimed 94% item-price association; on these clean renders the pipeline is at 100%, which is the ceiling for the synthetic set and not a number to expect on photographs. A good number on real menu photos would be 85-90% with the error log catching the rest.

Demo

  • Run: just headstorm_menu-setup && just headstorm_menu-up, open http://127.0.0.1:8118/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) click sample menu_02, read the headline and table; (2) click menu_05 (two columns) and check the JSON says "columns": 2; (3) open the Batch accordion, press "Run batch", read the accuracy line; (4) drop a real menu photo to see where it breaks.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__headstorm_menu.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: samples/menu_01.png to menu_05.png; menu_02 gives "Harbor Grill: 13 items, 13 with a price, 5 categories, 33 OCR boxes".

Limits and next steps

  • Synthetic menus only; photographed menus (shadows, curved pages, decorative fonts, multi-line descriptions) are untested and will be worse.
  • Two columns are handled, three or more and boxed layouts are not; LayoutLM-style document models are the next step.
  • The currency-glyph fix is a page-level heuristic; a real menu where most prices start with 8 and no $ is shown would be mis-corrected (prices >= 80 only).
  • No dedupe or normalisation across restaurants ("Fries" vs "French Fries"); that is the competitive-database step.
  • Throughput is about 8 s per menu on CPU; 1,000 menus is hours, not the 30 minutes claimed, until batched on a GPU.

title: Ops Inbox Triage Bot
one_liner: Paste an email and get category, urgency, a one-line summary and a suggested route, validated by pydantic, with the routing shown as simulated log lines.
body_html:
Ops Inbox Triage Bot

Brief

A shared ops inbox mixes sales leads, outages, invoice disputes, press requests and spam, and the lead that matters waits behind the noise. This bot reads one email and returns a structured record (category, urgency, summary, route) that a router can act on. Solved means every email is pre-sorted in seconds and the record is always on-schema, so downstream automation never sees a malformed answer.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv same as the rest of the portfolio
Model or core logic common/llm.py complete_json + pydantic EmailTriage provider by env, validation in code not in the prompt
Interface Streamlit with common/streamlit_theme.py two columns: email in, metrics and log out; key="input", key="run" for scripted demos
Data 6 sample emails with a hand-labelled category in triage.py one-click batch demo and a visible match count
Tests pytest (6) incl. AppTest smoke logic, validation, simulated routing, UI happy path

Libraries used

streamlit (UI), pydantic (schema validation, alias normalisation, route derivation), pandas (sample table), anthropic / openai / google-genai (providers behind the shared door), pytest, ruff.

How it was built

  1. Read the original triage_bot.py and app.py: OpenAI JSON mode, a fixed mock when no key, a success banner that claimed the email was "routed" with no routing code.
  2. Replaced the OpenAI call with common.llm.complete_json and a schema hint; renamed priority to urgency and added a Billing category and explicit route names (CRM, Slack #support, Slack #finance, Slack #partnerships, Ignore).
  3. Wrote EmailTriage validators: category and urgency aliases, route parsing, and a before-model validator that derives the route from the category when the model's route is missing or unknown.
  4. Added simulate_routing, which returns timestamped [SIMULATED] log lines instead of pretending to send.
  5. Built the Streamlit page: provider badge, Use sample, Triage, metrics, log, JSON, and a one-click table for all six samples with a match count.
  6. Tests (pure functions plus an AppTest run through sample -> Triage), ruff, just recipes with a pid file.

Results

No metrics file; the measurable part is the six-sample table. Offline (no key in the build environment) the match count is 1/6 because the door answers the first option (Sales) every time; it is the floor. With a key, 6/6 is expected on these clear cases. The tests prove: deterministic output, empty input rejected, URGENT -> High, slack:#support -> Slack #support, unknown route -> derived from category, every routing line labelled [SIMULATED], and the UI reaching a result from one click.

Demo

  • Run: just inbox_triage_bot-setup && just inbox_triage_bot-up, open http://localhost:8114/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) badge in the header; (2) Use sample -> Triage, read the three metrics and the [SIMULATED] log; (3) Triage all 6 samples, compare category with the label column; (4) paste a two-word email and show the record is still on-schema.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__inbox_triage_bot.webm.
  • Sample inputs: SAMPLE_EMAILS in triage.py (S1 sales lead, S2 outage, S3 duplicate invoice, S4 partnership, S5 spam, S6 API question). Offline every row is Sales / Low / CRM.

Limits and next steps

  • Routing is simulated by design; a production version adds real Slack and CRM clients behind an approval step.
  • Offline mode is a placeholder, not a classifier.
  • Six emails demonstrate the loop; a labelled set of a few hundred emails is needed to claim the 95% routing target.
  • No mailbox connector yet (Gmail/Outlook webhooks were the original next step and still are).

title: Internal Knowledge-Base Q&A
one_liner: Ask a policy question and get an answer that cites the file and chunk it came from, with retrieval done locally by MiniLM embeddings and a numpy cosine index, no hosted vector service.
body_html:
Internal Knowledge-Base Q&A

Brief

Employees lose time hunting through policy PDFs and wikis for a number or a deadline, and the answers they get from colleagues are often wrong. This app indexes the policy documents, finds the passages that match a question and answers with citations so the reader can verify every fact. Solved means a question about expenses, leave, security or remote work returns the right section in under a second, with the source next to it.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv same as the rest of the portfolio
Model or core logic sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (TF-IDF fallback) + numpy cosine index + lexical bonus; common/llm.py for the answer local, free, offline after one download; provider by env for the LLM step
Interface Streamlit with common/streamlit_theme.py question in, answer and citation expanders out; key="input", key="run"
Data docs/: 3 Markdown policies + 1 generated PDF, 18 chunks small, checkable, exercises both loaders
Tests pytest (5) incl. AppTest smoke loaders, chunking, index round trip, retrieval hits, offline citations, UI

Libraries used

sentence-transformers (MiniLM embeddings, cached in models/st/), scikit-learn (TF-IDF fallback), numpy (index and cosine search), pypdf (PDF text), streamlit (UI), anthropic / openai / google-genai (answer providers), reportlab (dev only: generated the sample PDF), pytest, ruff.

How it was built

  1. Read the original rag_pipeline.py: LangChain PyPDFLoader + RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, OpenAI embeddings, an in-memory Chroma store rebuilt on every question, RetrievalQA, and a hard-coded mock answer when docs/ was empty (it was empty).
  2. Wrote the four sample policies (expense, leave, IT security as Markdown; remote work generated as a PDF with reportlab) so there is something real to retrieve, with concrete numbers to check.
  3. Rewrote the pipeline in kb.py without LangChain: load_docs (md/txt/pdf), paragraph-aware chunk_text with word-boundary overlap, two embedders behind one interface, an Index that saves to models/kb_index/ and loads back, and answer, which prompts for [file chunk N] citations through common/llm.py.
  4. Added a lexical bonus to the cosine score after noticing MiniLM tied the "Leave of absence" section with a neighbouring chunk; the exact-phrase section now ranks first.
  5. Built the Streamlit page: provider and embedder badges, indexed documents with chunk counts, Use sample, Ask, answer, citation expanders with scores, Rebuild index.
  6. Tests run with TF-IDF in a temporary index dir so they need no download; just kb-index builds the MiniLM index.

Results

On this machine: 18 chunks from 4 files, MiniLM, index build about 15 s including model load, search under 50 ms. Retrieval on the four sample questions is 4/4 (top chunk is the right section for leave of absence, expense submission, stolen laptop, working abroad), checked by the tests with TF-IDF and by hand with MiniLM. This is a sanity check, not the >85% precision claim: that needs a labelled question set of a few hundred. The hallucination rate cannot be measured without a key; the prompt restricts the model to the excerpts and the page flags answers without citation markers.

Demo

  • Run: just internal_kb_qa-setup && just kb-index && just internal_kb_qa-up, open http://localhost:8113/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) sidebar: badge, minilm, 18 chunks, four files; (2) Use sample -> Ask, read the "Leave of absence" passage and its citation; (3) open the citation expanders and show the scores; (4) click the "work from another country" sample to show a hit inside the PDF.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__internal_kb_qa.webm.
  • Sample inputs: SAMPLE_QUESTIONS in kb.py; expected top files are leave_policy.md, expense_policy.md, remote_work_policy.pdf, it_security_policy.md.

Limits and next steps

  • Offline, the answer is the best passage, not generated text; a key turns on the written, cited answer.
  • Four fictional documents; a real deployment points KB_DOCS_DIR at the policy folder and rebuilds.
  • Scores are not calibrated: an off-topic question still returns passages, and only the prompt stops the model from answering from them.
  • Text only; tables and images in PDFs are skipped. A reranker and a labelled eval set are the next steps.

title: Model Monitoring API
one_liner: The churn model served by FastAPI with Prometheus request, latency and score histograms, plus a z-score drift check on the last 200 inputs.
body_html:
Model Monitoring API

Brief

A model that is accurate on the day it ships can quietly degrade: slower responses, inputs that no longer look like the training set, a score distribution that piles up at one end. This service wraps a real prediction model so every request is counted and timed for Prometheus and the input stream can be checked for drift on demand. "Solved" means an operator sees a problem on the status page or in /metrics before a customer does.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv Same as the rest of the portfolio
Model or core logic The churn champion pipeline from ../churn_predictor/models/churn.joblib (scikit-learn 1.9) The monitored model is a real one, not a random number
Interface FastAPI + one HTML status page on common/ui.css /predict, /metrics, /drift, /health, /simulate with OpenAPI docs for free
Data Training statistics stored in the bundle; traffic generated by random_customer() Drift needs the training means and stds; traffic is simulated
Tests pytest + FastAPI TestClient (6 tests) predict, validation, metrics text, drift numbers, shifted traffic flagged

Libraries used

fastapi (routing, validation), prometheus_client (Counter, Histogram, /metrics ASGI app), pydantic (customer schema with enum fields), joblib + scikit-learn (load and run the churn pipeline), pandas (one-row frames, drift means), uvicorn (server), requests (load script), httpx (TestClient), ruff, pytest.

How it was built

  1. The original main.py had the right shape (Counter, latency Histogram, score Histogram, middleware, /metrics mount) but /predict returned random.random() after a random sleep, and simulate_load.py only printed status codes. The metric names and middleware were kept.
  2. /predict now loads the churn bundle by path and runs the champion pipeline; the request body is a typed Customer with validated enum values and defaults, so a minimal JSON works and a wrong contract type is a 422.
  3. Added /drift: a rolling deque of the last 200 inputs; for each numeric feature a z-score of the recent mean against the training mean with the standard error of the mean, |z| > 3 flags it; categoricals compare level shares.
  4. Added /simulate (in-process traffic with an optional shift), /summary, /health, and the status page with stat tiles, a score histogram and the drift table; simulate_load.py fires 200 real HTTP requests and prints p50/p95/p99.
  5. Tests train the churn model through its own venv if the bundle is missing, so the suite runs from a clean checkout.

Results

Measured on this machine against the running service (just model_monitoring_api-load):

Measure Value
HTTP latency p50 / p95 / p99 7.99 / 13.33 / 14.93 ms
Throughput, one sequential client 114 req/s
Random traffic drift stable (all
Shifted traffic (+36 months, +$60) drift, Tenure and TotalCharges z > 3

p99 under 15 ms clears the original "p99 < 100 ms" target with room to spare; a good production number for a tabular model behind an HTTP hop is anything under about 50 ms.

Demo

  • Run: just model_monitoring_api-setup && just model_monitoring_api-up, open http://127.0.0.1:8115/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) "Fire 50 requests": tiles, histogram and a green drift table; (2) "Fire 50 drifted requests" twice: Tenure and TotalCharges go amber, status drift; (3) score one customer in the form; (4) open /metrics and find model_prediction_score_bucket.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__model_monitoring_api.webm (recorded by just demo-video).
  • Sample inputs: the two buttons; or curl -X POST localhost:8115/predict -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"Tenure": 2, "MonthlyCharges": 110, "Contract": "Month-to-month"}' returns about 0.93.

Limits and next steps

  • Traffic is simulated; there is no real client and no Prometheus or Grafana running, only the scrape text.
  • The rolling window is in-process memory: it resets on restart and is per worker. Production would push to a metrics store or run the drift job over a request log.
  • The drift test is a mean shift z-test; it misses variance changes and multivariate drift. Evidently or a PSI/KS per feature would be the next step.
  • No auth, no rate limiting, no model version in the response beyond the model name.

title: Support Ticket Classifier
one_liner: A FastAPI endpoint that turns a raw support ticket into validated JSON (tags, priority, next action) through a provider-agnostic LLM door, with an eval script that scores it.
body_html:
Support Ticket Classifier

Brief

Support teams lose about a fifth of their time reading tickets just to tag and prioritise them before anyone can act. This service takes the ticket text and returns tags, a priority and one suggested next step as JSON that a routing system can consume. Solved means a triage queue that is pre-labelled, measured against hand labels, and cheap enough to run on every ticket.

Tech stack

Layer Choice Why
Language and runtime Python 3.11 via uv one lockfile, same across the portfolio
Model or core logic common/llm.py complete_json (Anthropic Haiku default; OpenAI / Gemini via env; offline fallback) no provider code in the app, no key in source, tests run with no network
Interface FastAPI + one HTML page on common/ui.css no build step; #input, #run, #result for scripted demos
Data examples.json, 8 hand-labelled tickets enough for a smoke eval; the eval script scales to a larger file
Tests pytest + FastAPI TestClient (7 tests) API, validation, HTML page, eval file

Libraries used

fastapi (routes and OpenAPI), uvicorn (server), pydantic (TicketResult validation and normalisation), anthropic / openai / google-genai (providers behind the shared door), httpx (TestClient), pytest, ruff.

How it was built

  1. Read the original main.py: OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo in JSON mode, eval() on the model output, a hard-coded mock when the key was missing, and a JSON root route. The README promised >90% accuracy with no eval.
  2. Moved the LLM call to common/llm.py with a schema hint (tags, priority, suggested_action); dropped the OpenAI SDK import and the eval().
  3. Added TicketResult validators: tags lowercased and de-duplicated, unknown priorities fall back to Medium, empty tags become other, and the response carries provider and model so the UI can show what answered.
  4. Wrote the HTML page (textarea, eight one-click sample tickets, result card, raw JSON, provider badge) on the shared ui.css, plus /health, /examples and /static.
  5. Wrote eval.py: priority accuracy, micro tag precision/recall/F1, exact match, latency, written to models/metrics.json; it runs offline (deterministic floor) and with a key (real score).
  6. Tests and ruff; just recipes for setup, test, up (pid file), down and eval.

Results

From models/metrics.json on this machine, offline mode (no key available in the build environment):

Metric Offline What a good number is
priority_accuracy 0.25 > 0.85
tag_f1 (micro) 0.222 > 0.90
exact_match 0.0 > 0.75
mean_latency_s 0.0 < 2 s with a real model

Offline, the door answers the first option of every field, so 0.25 is the share of tickets labelled Low and the tag score is the share tagged billing. The real number needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... just ticket_classifier-eval, which overwrites the file with the provider and model named inside it.

Demo

  • Run: just ticket_classifier-setup && just ticket_classifier-up, open http://localhost:8112/.
  • Two-minute walkthrough: (1) read the header badge, it says offline or the model name; (2) click sample #2, the outage ticket, and look at priority and tags in the result card; (3) click sample #6, a two-tag ticket, and show the raw JSON; (4) curl localhost:8112/health and open models/metrics.json.
  • Video clip: demo/clips/portfolio__ticket_classifier.webm.
  • Sample inputs: examples.json (8 tickets with gold tags and priority). Offline, every ticket returns billing / Low with a placeholder action; with a key, #2 and #5 should come back Urgent, #3 Low.

Limits and next steps

  • Offline mode is a placeholder, not a classifier; it exists so the demo and tests never need a key.
  • Eight examples measure plumbing, not accuracy; a 200-ticket labelled set with a confusion matrix is the next step.
  • No few-shot examples in the prompt yet; tag drift on niche technical tickets is the known weak spot.
  • Routing after classification (CRM, queue) is not built; the API is the contract for it.
